pw3: 💡 Portion the yogurt and frozen berries into tubs for up to 4 days; the berries thaw overnight and bleed a little juice, which is fine, but bag the granola separately so it stays crunchy.
💡 Eat this 60 to 75 minutes before training so the yogurt has time to sit; if your session is closer than that, halve the yogurt and keep the berries and honey for faster carbs.
pw5: 💡 Stir each jar again after 10 minutes so the chia and protein powder hydrate evenly rather than settling into a dense layer at the bottom; the jars keep 4 days chilled.
💡 Add the banana only on the morning you eat it, as sliced banana browns and turns mushy in the fridge, and microwave for 60 seconds at 600 W if you prefer it warm.
pw1: 💡 Rice cakes go chewy within an hour of being spread, so store the peanut butter and honey portioned in small pots and build the stack no more than 15 minutes before eating.
💡 Use a fully spotted banana here; the riper it is, the faster its sugars digest, which matters when you are eating 30 to 45 minutes before a session.
sm1: 💡 Soak the oats in the milk for 10 minutes before blending so they break down fully instead of leaving a gritty texture; blend the dates first if your blender is a low-powered one.
💡 This shake thickens noticeably after a night in the fridge as the oats swell, so if you batch it, loosen with 50 ml extra milk and shake hard before drinking within 24 hours.
sm2: 💡 Freeze the banana and dates in a bag the night before; frozen fruit gives a thick, cold shake without ice diluting the cocoa and peanut flavour.
💡 Drink this within 60 to 90 minutes after training, or 2 hours before, as 16 g fat from the peanut butter sits heavily if taken right before lifting.
sm3: 💡 Blend the kale, spinach and liquid on high for 30 seconds before adding the fruit, otherwise the tough kale stems leave fibrous flecks through the finished smoothie.
💡 Portion the banana, pineapple and greens into freezer bags for up to 3 months; tip a bag into the blender with the coconut milk and protein for a 2-minute breakfast.
sm4: 💡 At under 4 g fat and 30 g protein, this is your fastest-digesting smoothie in the set, so it works as a post-session drink within 30 minutes of finishing.
💡 Blend the frozen berries with only half the coconut water first, then add the rest with the yogurt and whey; a small pour of liquid to start stops the blades spinning freely above the fruit.
sm5: 💡 Sift the matcha into warm water, not hot, and whisk to a paste before it meets the milk; dry matcha added straight to the blender clumps and leaves bitter green specks.
💡 Fresh strawberries make this thin, so pour it over ice immediately rather than storing it, as the whey and milk separate into layers within a few hours in the fridge.
sm6: 💡 Peanut butter powder and cocoa both clump against the blender wall, so add them on top of the liquid and banana, never first, and scrape down once halfway through.
💡 Pour into an ice-cube tray and freeze for a month; five cubes blended with a splash of almond milk gives a thick shake for after training without any extra prep.
sm7: 💡 With 60 g whey in only 100 ml coconut milk this is very thick, so use frozen mango and banana for texture but add 100 ml cold water if your blender labours.
💡 Shake any leftover well before drinking within 24 hours; the coconut fat rises and sets in a layer at the top when it is chilled.
sm8: 💡 Cool the espresso for 5 minutes before it goes into the blender; hot coffee poured onto whey makes it seize into lumps and can curdle the milk.
💡 Blend and freeze in a lidded cup the night before a morning session, then let it thaw for 20 minutes; drink it 45 to 60 minutes before training so the caffeine lands during your warm-up.
sm9: 💡 Add the almond butter and whey last so they sit on top of the frozen berries; if they land in the base first they glue themselves under the blades and never mix in.
💡 Skip the dates at first and taste before adjusting; frozen berry mixes vary in sweetness and the banana alone often carries it, saving 60 kcal a serving.
sn3: 💡 Chop the fruit up to 2 days ahead and keep it in a sealed tub, but add the lime, chilli and salt only just before eating; salt draws water from watermelon and turns the bowl soupy.
💡 Eat this 30 to 40 minutes before a session; at 2 g protein and 1 g fat it clears the stomach quickly, and it does not freeze well, so do not batch beyond 2 days.
sn4: 💡 Keep the beetroot in its own tub or it stains every other vegetable pink within an hour; the julienned veg keeps 3 days chilled in cold water, drained and patted dry before serving.
💡 Let the quick-pickled carrot and onion sit at least 10 minutes in the vinegar and a good pinch of salt; unpickled raw onion is harsh against the mild cottage cheese.
sn5: 💡 Assemble this no more than an hour ahead: watermelon leaks juice into the yogurt base and the balsamic glaze bleeds into everything, so keep the components in separate pots if prepping.
💡 Let the steamed edamame cool fully before it touches the yogurt, and crumble the feta over last so its salt hits the watermelon at the moment of eating rather than drawing it out.
sn7: 💡 The baba ganoush keeps 4 days chilled and freezes well; the whey tzatziki keeps 3 days but must stay cold, and the chickpeas lose their crunch in a tub, so re-crisp them 3 minutes at 200°C in the air fryer.
💡 Prick the aubergine skin before roasting and let it drain in a colander for 10 minutes after scooping; skipping this leaves watery, bitter baba that soaks straight through the pita.
bf17: 💡 Whisk the whey into the yogurt with a fork and let it sit 5 minutes before stirring again; the powder needs time to hydrate and the second stir removes any last lumps.
💡 Assemble the yogurt, chia and berries the night before if you like, as the berries thaw into the base by morning, but keep the granola and honey off until you eat.
bf18: 💡 If the bowl comes out thin enough to drink, add 30 g more frozen berries and pulse rather than adding ice; watery bowls send the granola to the bottom and soggy in minutes.
💡 Blend and freeze the base in a tub for up to a month, then let it sit out 15 minutes before scooping; it eats like sorbet and gives the toppings a firm surface to sit on.
bf19: 💡 Freeze the mango and banana in chunks first; using them fresh gives a thin, room-temperature purée that will not hold the granola on top.
💡 Stop blending as soon as it is smooth, as the extra minute warms the yogurt and turns the texture from thick and scoopable into a loose smoothie.
bf22: 💡 Whisk the whey into the cold coconut water before the oats go in; dry powder added to already-soaked oats leaves pockets of paste, and the jar keeps 4 days sealed in the fridge.
💡 Dice the mango and toast the almonds up to 3 days ahead in separate pots, adding them and the granola only at breakfast so the crunch survives and the mango does not weep into the oats.
bf24: 💡 Roll this fresh: the yogurt layer makes the tortilla soften within a couple of hours, so if you must prep, keep the whey yogurt in a pot and assemble in 2 minutes at breakfast.
💡 Warm the tortilla just enough to bend without cracking, then let it cool 30 seconds before spreading the yogurt; residual heat on a whey mixture makes it turn thin and slightly grainy.
m68: 💡 Store the shredded chicken and cabbage together for up to 3 days, but keep the vinaigrette, cashews and wonton strips in separate pots; dressed cabbage weeps and softens within a few hours.
💡 Poach the chicken at a bare simmer, never a rolling boil, and pull it at 74°C on a probe; boiled breast shreds into dry strands that the dressing cannot rescue.
m69: 💡 The roasted pumpkin, chickpeas and massaged kale keep 4 days chilled; reheat only the pumpkin and chickpeas, 3 minutes at 200°C in an air fryer, and keep the cottage cheese, feta and tortilla chips separate.
💡 Spread the pumpkin cubes in a single layer with space between them; a crowded tray steams instead of roasting and you get pale, soft cubes with no caramelised edges.
ds3: 💡 The filled tarts keep 3 days in the fridge and freeze for a month; eat them straight from frozen after 20 minutes on the bench, as full defrosting makes the oat crust soften.
💡 Press the crust firmly up the sides of the mould with the back of a spoon and chill the full 30 minutes; a loosely packed base crumbles the moment you lift the tart out.
ds4: 💡 Pull the tin at 20 minutes when the centre still wobbles slightly; whey-based batters dry out fast, and 3 extra minutes takes them from fudgy to rubbery.
💡 Cut into 8 squares once fully cold, then wrap and freeze for up to 2 months; a 15-second microwave burst on medium brings a frozen square back to fudgy.
sn9: 💡 Assemble on the day: drained tuna keeps 2 days in a sealed tub in the fridge, but cut tomatoes and cucumber weep and go soft overnight, so slice them fresh.
💡 Salt the tomato slices a few minutes before plating and drain off the liquid; that small step stops the plate turning into a puddle by the time you finish the tuna.
pw7: 💡 Slice and freeze the bagels the day you buy them, then toast straight from frozen; a week-old bagel from the bread bin is stale by day three.
💡 Eat 30 to 45 minutes before running with the honey and banana as written; skip adding peanut butter or cheese, since the fat slows the carbs you want available for the session.
ds5: 💡 Check with a skewer at 45 minutes and tent with foil if the top browns before the centre sets; the whey and honey brown quickly and a dark crust does not mean it is cooked.
💡 Slice the cooled loaf and freeze the slices between squares of baking paper for up to 3 months; 20 seconds in the microwave at 600 W softens one from frozen.
ds6: 💡 Blend the cottage cheese for the full 60 seconds and scrape down twice; stopping early leaves tiny curds that make the mousse taste of cheese rather than chocolate.
💡 The mousse keeps 4 days chilled under its shell but does not freeze, and the chocolate cracks cleanly only if the mousse is fridge-cold before you pour it over.
bf34: 💡 Bake a tray of six ramekins at once and keep them covered in the fridge for 4 days; 60 seconds in the microwave brings one back to soft and warm.
💡 Mash the banana completely smooth and check the baking powder is fresh; lumpy banana leaves wet pockets and old baking powder gives a dense, flat oat cake.
m109: 💡 Meatballs and sauce keep 4 days chilled or 3 months frozen; reheat gently in a covered pan with a splash of water rather than the microwave, which tightens the ground chicken.
💡 Store the jasmine rice in its own tub and reheat it separately with a wet paper towel over it; rice left sitting in coconut curry overnight absorbs the sauce and turns gluey.
m113: 💡 Caramelise a full batch of onions at once, 5 or 6 onions on low for 40 minutes, and portion them into 75 g pots; they keep a week chilled or freeze for 3 months.
💡 Store the seared, sliced steak separately for up to 3 days and build the sandwich fresh; toast it in a dry pan under a weight, as a pre-assembled one goes limp from the horseradish yogurt.
m120: 💡 Keep the sauce and salmon together for 2 days at most, and reheat in a covered pan on low with a spoon of water; the microwave overcooks the fish and splits the yogurt.
💡 If the evaporated milk sauce reduces too far it turns sticky, so pull it while it still runs off the spoon; it thickens again once the spinach and yogurt go in.
m122: 💡 Blend the cottage cheese sauce in a batch and keep it 4 days chilled; it thickens in the fridge, so loosen with warm pasta water or milk over low heat and never let it boil.
💡 Undercook the rigatoni by a minute if batching, and store the pasta, sauce and sliced steak in three tubs; combined, the pasta swells and the sauce goes claggy by day two.
m123: 💡 The gravy-coated chicken keeps 4 days chilled and freezes well, but the mash goes gluey in the microwave; reheat it in a pan with a splash of milk, and keep the beans separate to re-char.
💡 Cook the mushrooms until their liquid has fully evaporated and they are browned, not grey; wet mushrooms water down the gravy and it will never thicken properly, whatever the cornstarch does.
ds7: 💡 Keep the bars frozen in a sealed tub with baking paper between layers for up to a month; eat within 3 minutes of taking one out, as the banana turns mushy once it thaws.
💡 Let the melted chocolate cool for 2 minutes before drizzling; poured straight from the microwave it melts the peanut butter layer and slides off the frozen banana instead of setting.
